paras: The threatened lynching of Will Horn took place on August 17, 1905, when a mob was reported forming at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, to lynch Horn after his capture, and Governor Vardaman sent troops to take him away. Horn, a Black convict charged in the killing of J. G. Smith, the white man in charge of the city convict force, was carried under military guard to the Jackson jail, and no attack was made. Two other Black men had already been lynched at Hattiesburg over Smith's death, and Horn was later quoted as saying one of them was innocent.

On August 4, 1905, according to an Associated Press dispatch, Smith, described as "an aged white man in charge of the city convict force," was shot and killed by William Horn, one of the Black prisoners in his gang, who escaped into nearby woods. The New-York Tribune said Horn and "Kid" George attacked Smith together, and that George and Ed Lewis, alias Brock, were jailed and that night hanged to a bridge by a mob. Writing of that lynching on August 17, the Oklahoma Safeguard noted that Horn "escaped and up to this writing he has not been caught."

On the afternoon of August 17, Governor Vardaman was informed by telegraph that Horn had been captured between Lumberton and Hattiesburg and was in the charge of Sheriff Moody and a posse. He was also told that "a mob was being formed at Hattiesburg to lynch Horn." Vardaman ordered Adjutant General Fridge at Gulfport to take troops and bring Horn to Jackson for safekeeping, and Fridge left on a special train to relieve the sheriff, who was "hiding the negro in the woods."

According to a special dispatch to the St. Louis Republic, forty soldiers under Fridge and Major Virgil Jones reached Jackson with Horn at 8 o'clock that night. The same dispatch said a movement had been on foot at Hattiesburg to lynch Horn on his arrival, but no attempt was made when the train pulled in "with the car windows bristling with Krag-Jorgensen rifles." Vardaman met the train at the Jackson depot and thanked the soldiers, and Horn was turned over to Sheriff Spann of Hinds County and jailed.

The St. Louis Republic reported that Horn made "a full confession" implicating four other prisoners besides the two men already lynched. A brief in Indiana and Ohio weeklies a week later had Horn admitting the killing but saying he never intended to kill and that one of the lynched men was innocent. In early September two Mississippi papers reported that Horn, still in the Jackson jail, had been declared insane, The Leader calling him "a raving maniac." No report of a trial, or of any action against those who organized the Hattiesburg mob, appears in the coverage.

White papers framed the story as a lynching prevented: the Montgomery Advertiser headed the Associated Press dispatch "Vardaman Acts Promptly," and the Newport News Daily Press ran it as "Trying to Head Off Judge Lynch." The St. Louis Republic's headline read "Forty Soldiers Prevent Lynching of Negro by Mob," though its text called Horn "the negro desperado who assassinated" Smith, stating the charge as fact.

The Plymouth Tribune and the Hocking Sentinel led with Horn's own claim under the headline "Innocent Men Were Lynched." Mississippi papers treated Horn as a murderer: the Clarion-Ledger, quoted in The Leader, said he "led the murderous assault," and the Ellisville New South-News said he "murdered the foreman of the chain gang."

The Black papers covered the August 4 lynching; no Black-press report of Horn's capture or of the troops appears in the coverage. The Oklahoma Safeguard said the guilty deserved death but declared, "We have never favored lynching nor do we now," holding that the mob had been wrong to take the law into its own hands.

Accounts differ on Horn's part: the first wire report named him as the man who fired, the New-York Tribune said he and George acted together, and the August 17 dispatch spoke only of "complicity." A Clarion-Ledger item credited the Lumberton military company with escorting Horn, while the same-day Jackson dispatches, closer to the event, named Fridge's detail from Gulfport.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Will Horn
bases: A mob was reported forming at Hattiesburg to lynch Horn, a Black prisoner, and troops were sent to carry him to Jackson; no attack was made (A10, A11, A12).

Horn was not killed: a mob was reported forming to lynch him over the killing of guard J. G. Smith, but troops took him to the Jackson jail and no attempt was made (A11, A12); this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The AP Jackson dispatch (A10, A12), a separate St. Louis Republic special (A11) and a Daily Clarion-Ledger item (A16) agree that Horn was captured and taken to Jackson under military guard to keep him from a mob.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser headed the AP dispatch 'Vardaman Acts Promptly. By Sending Troops Mississippi Governor Prevents Lynching.'
The Newport News Daily Press ran the same dispatch as 'Trying to Head Off Judge Lynch', protecting the 'Negro From Wrath of Mob'.
The St. Louis Republic's 'Forty Soldiers Prevent Lynching of Negro by Mob' praised the rescue while calling Horn 'the negro desperado who assassinated' Smith.
The Plymouth Tribune and Hocking Sentinel led with Horn's claim under 'Innocent Men Were Lynched'.
Mississippi papers reported Horn's jailing and insanity, stating as fact that he 'murdered' Smith.
The Oklahoma Safeguard, on the August 4 lynching that preceded Horn's capture, declared 'We have never favored lynching nor do we now.'
